readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module takes the AWS Global Infrastructure beyond the basics of Regions and Availability Zones. It explains how to pick a Region, how multi-AZ and multi-Region designs keep applications available, and how edge locations with Amazon CloudFront bring content closer to users. It closes with infrastructure as code, using AWS CloudFormation to build the same environment anywhere, and compares it with the console and programmatic access.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 4 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Going Global: the coffee shop's move abroad as a map of Region choice, edge locations and IaC.

AWS Global Infrastructure

  1. Choosing AWS Regions: the four Region selection factors of compliance, proximity, feature availability and pricing.
  2. Diving Deeper into AWS Global Infrastructure: multi-AZ and multi-Region redundancy, edge locations, CloudFront, Route 53 and Outposts.
  3. Infrastructure and Automation: infrastructure as code with CloudFormation, and when to use the console, the CLI, SDKs or IaC.

Module 4 Conclusion

The Assessment and Module Summary lessons have no notes files of their own; they feed the assessment and summary sections below.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Choose a Region by checking compliance first, then weighing proximity, feature availability and pricing.
  • Regions are isolated, data leaves one only with your permission, and the host country's laws apply to it.
  • A Region holds three or more AZs, and each AZ is one or more data centers with independent power, networking and connectivity.
  • Multi-AZ and multi-Region designs give high availability, fault tolerance and low latency for end users.
  • High availability, agility and elasticity are separate benefits of the global infrastructure.
  • Edge locations sit outside Regions and cache content for higher transfer speeds and lower latency, while Regions host most AWS services.
  • CloudFront runs on edge locations, which also host Route 53 and Global Accelerator.
  • AWS Outposts runs AWS services on premises when even a Region plus CloudFront is too slow.
  • CloudFormation models and sets up resources from code, giving identical environments across Regions and accounts with fewer errors.
  • Programmatic access suits developers, the console suits newcomers and visual tasks, and IaC suits repeatable, consistent multi-Region deployments.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

The module widened the view of the AWS Global Infrastructure along three lines. First came deciding where to deploy, then why edge locations are worth having, and finally letting services like CloudFormation make deployments faster and automatic.

Notes

What the module adds

  • On top of Regions and Availability Zones (AZs), the module covers Region selection, edge locations, and automated deployment with .
  • Together these give a business elasticity and agility, not only .
  • The end goal is applications that are robust, scalable and reachable worldwide.

The coffee shop goes international

  • New shops: where to open depends on local demand, rules and costs, just as several factors decide which AWS Regions to use.
  • Coffee carts: small, light outlets sell only the best sellers, fast, like edge locations.
  • Edge locations cache popular images, videos and other assets near users, so nobody waits for a trip to a central location.
  • Same drink everywhere: shared recipes and machine settings copied to every shop keep the product identical, like with CloudFormation.
  • IaC lets a business grow responsibly, with matching deployments across environments and Regions.

Visuals

Key takeaways

  • Region choice is a multi-factor business decision, unpacked in Choosing AWS Regions.
  • Edge locations serve frequently requested content quickly from a cache close to users.
  • IaC with CloudFormation repeats the same reliable setup each time the business grows.

Terms

  • Edge location: A small AWS site that caches popular content close to users.
  • Infrastructure as code (IaC): Defining infrastructure in files so deployments are automated and alike.
  • AWS CloudFormation: The AWS IaC service for automating resource deployment.

choosing-aws-regions.html:
Choosing AWS Regions

Objectives

  • Explain what to weigh when selecting one or more AWS Regions.

Notes

Regions are isolated

  • Isolation is a security feature: each Region is walled off from all others, and data crosses that line only with your explicit permission.
  • Data in a Region is bound by the host country's laws.

The four factors

Factor What to check
Compliance Laws and data protection rules on where data may live
Proximity Distance to most users, as nearer means lower and snappier apps
Feature availability Whether needed services exist there yet, since features roll out gradually
Pricing Operating and energy costs, local taxes and tax incentives
  • Check compliance first, since a legal rule can settle the Region alone, but most businesses have none and move on to the rest.
  • Under , the EU privacy law, an EU online shop must get consent before collecting personal data and let people see or erase it.
  • A distant Region adds delay, which can hurt user satisfaction and overall efficiency.
  • carry strict physical, operational and personnel controls for US government bodies and contractors.
  • AWS pricing is transparent and granular, yet each Region has its own rates.
  • may force data to stay in the country, which touches both compliance and cost.
  • Uptime and performance are broadly equal across Regions, and licensing or hardware specs are on-premises concerns.

Key takeaways

  • The four factors are compliance, proximity, feature availability and pricing.
  • Compliance comes first and can decide alone; the other three have no fixed ranking.
  • Regions are isolated, follow local law, and differ in services and prices.

Scenarios

  • Frankfurt financial data that German law keeps in-country -> compliance decides.
  • UK-only or China-only data -> the London Region or a Region in China.
  • Customers mostly in Singapore -> the Singapore Region, not Virginia.
  • EU online retailer -> GDPR compliance.
  • US government workload -> AWS GovCloud Regions.
  • The knowledge check practised weighing compliance and proximity for a public-sector workload.

Terms

  • Latency: The delay as data travels between users and the hosting site.
  • General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR): The EU regulation protecting personal data and privacy.
  • AWS GovCloud Regions: Regions with strict security controls for US government agencies and their contractors.
  • Data sovereignty laws: Laws requiring data to be stored locally.

diving-deeper-into-aws-global-infrastruc.html:
Diving Deeper into AWS Global Infrastructure

Objectives

  • Explain the benefits of multi-Region and multi-AZ deployments.
  • Say what an is.
  • Tell Regions, AZs and edge locations apart.

Notes

Redundancy for uptime

  • A redundant architecture replicates resources across layers of AWS infrastructure so backups take over, for long-term stability and near-zero downtime.
  • With and , resources keep working when one hosting location fails.
  • Multi-AZ covers one AZ failing: the app moves to a backup AZ you set up, with quicker disaster recovery, continuity, lower latency and compliance as bonuses.
  • Multi-Region goes one step further and survives a whole Region going down.
  • The infrastructure also brings and (see Terms).

Edge locations

  • The Amazon Global Edge Network brings AWS services and content to users beyond standard Regions with low latency.
  • Edge locations sit apart from Regions, in spots like Atlanta and Shanghai, and cache data, video and apps for higher transfer speeds and lower latency.
  • Regions run most AWS services; edge locations are not for heavy compute, databases or redundant storage.
  • , a and cache, uses them to serve images, video, apps and APIs near users.
  • They also host and , a service that routes users to internet apps by turning URLs into IP addresses.
  • For more speed than a Region plus CloudFront, runs AWS services on premises.

Regions vs AZs vs edge locations

Layer Made of Role
Region Data centers in one geographic area, split into three or more AZs Scalable, redundant hosting for most AWS services
AZ One or more data centers with their own power, networking and connectivity High availability and fault tolerance, isolated from failures elsewhere
Edge location A caching site outside any Region or AZ Fast content delivery for the AWS CDN

Visuals

  • Key elements of : three markers placing AZs inside Regions and edge locations apart, as the table shows.

Key takeaways

  • Multi-AZ and multi-Region designs give high availability, fault tolerance and low latency for end users.
  • A Region has three or more AZs, and each AZ has one or more data centers.
  • Edge locations sit outside Regions and cache content for lower latency and faster transfers.

Scenarios

  • AZ or Region outage -> switch to a configured backup AZ or another Region.
  • Slow-loading images in the shop's app -> CloudFront.
  • The knowledge check practised matching each layer to its definition.

Terms

  • High availability: Running without failing, riding out component failures without significant downtime.
  • Fault tolerance: Staying operational when a hosting location has an outage.
  • Agility: Adapting fast to change, such as by redeploying services quickly.
  • Elasticity: Scaling resources up or down automatically with demand.
  • Amazon CloudFront: The AWS content delivery network (CDN), running on edge locations.
  • Amazon Route 53: The AWS DNS service that maps URLs to IP addresses.
  • AWS Outposts: Running AWS services on premises.

infrastructure-and-automation.html:
Infrastructure and Automation

Objectives

  • Explain what CloudFormation does and why teams use it.
  • Match , the console and to their use cases.

Notes

Why automate

  • Rebuilding a Region's resources elsewhere by hand is slow, risky and hard to repeat.
  • Infrastructure as code (IaC) stores the architecture as a source-controlled blueprint that tools rebuild anywhere, identically and easily.

AWS CloudFormation

  • CloudFormation models and sets up AWS resources from code, freeing time for apps.
  • Its templates are text files declaring what to build, not how, and it provisions and configures it all through AWS APIs.
  • One template across accounts or Regions gives identical environments from one command, with fewer errors and more resilience.
  • It handles simple to complex multi-tier apps with intricate dependencies and, once learned, speeds deployment.
  • It is not a click-by-click visual tool, a content cache (edge locations do that) or a cost optimizer.

Four ways to call AWS APIs

Approach Suits Typical use
Coders Many services from one command line; scripted routine jobs like backups
AWS SDKs App developers One app step, like saving to Amazon Simple Storage Service ()
Console Cloud newcomers Search, simple workflows, billing dashboards, graphical services (, )
IaC Organization-wide automation DevOps continuous integration and delivery () pipelines; consistent multi-Region scaling of
  • For consistent multi-Region rollouts, the console fits only small one-off jobs, scripts automate partly but get hard to maintain, and mixing methods causes drift.
  • IaC is , so teams can version, review and automate deployments.

Visuals

  • Interacting with AWS resources: three markers matching each approach to its users and uses.

Key takeaways

  • CloudFormation builds resources from code, cutting errors and keeping environments consistent.
  • For consistent multi-Region rollouts, IaC beats the console, scripts or a mix.
  • Programmatic access suits developers, the console newcomers, and IaC repeatable work at scale.

Scenarios

  • Copying Region A's setup to Region B -> one .
  • The knowledge check practised picking CloudFormation for a complex EC2, and Auto Scaling stack.

Terms

  • CloudFormation template: A text document declaring the resources to build.
  • Declarative: Stating what should exist, not how to build it.
  • Programmatic access: Using AWS through code, with the AWS CLI or SDKs.

labs.title: Choose the Region
labs.brief: A data sovereignty law in the cafe's country says the loyalty records of its customers must stay at home, and the new order app cannot run without a service that not every Region offers yet. The law comes first, and the owner will pay a little more for a faster app, so pick the Region that keeps the records home, runs the service and sits nearest the customers. Every latency and price below is a lab value, and prices are in lab credits.

options.label: Ashcombe
options.detail: Data is kept abroad. 63 ms to customers. Runs the order service. 10 lab credits an hour.

options.label: Farhaven
options.detail: Data is kept abroad. 88 ms to customers. Runs the order service. 5 lab credits an hour.

options.label: Harbour Point
options.detail: Data stays in the cafe's country. 6 ms to customers. Order service not offered yet. 8 lab credits an hour.

options.label: Millbrook
options.detail: Data stays in the cafe's country. 14 ms to customers. Runs the order service. 9 lab credits an hour.

options.label: Stonegate
options.detail: Data stays in the cafe's country. 41 ms to customers. Runs the order service. 7 lab credits an hour.

goals.label: The loyalty records stay inside the cafe's country
goals.hint: A law about where data may live can settle the choice on its own, so check where each Region keeps the data before any other factor.

goals.label: The lawful Region also runs the service the app needs
goals.hint: New services reach Regions a few at a time, so a Region that obeys the law may still be unable to host the app today.

goals.label: Of the lawful Regions with the service, the nearest one
goals.hint: Among the Regions still in the running, the one closest to the customers cuts the delay they feel each time they order.

lines: The cheapest Region was out before price came into it, because a data sovereignty law can force data to stay in the country.
The nearest lawful Region could not host the app, since services arrive in each Region over time and it lacked the one the app needs.
After compliance no factor has a fixed rank, so the cafe's own needs set the order, and here the app cannot run without its service and the owner puts speed ahead of price.
Each Region has its own rates, so the nearest lawful Region with the service cost more than a slower one, a trade the owner chose to make.

questions.takeaway: Compliance is checked first because a data location law can decide the Region by itself.

read.text: Check compliance first, since a legal rule can settle the Region alone, but most businesses have none and move on to the rest.

options.text: Compliance
options.why: A law on where data may live can rule out every other Region before anything else is weighed.

options.text: Feature availability

options.text: Each Region has its own local costs and taxes
options.why: Operating and energy costs, local taxes and tax incentives vary by Region, so rates vary too.

options.text: Each Region gets new features on its own schedule
options.why: Gradual feature rollout affects which services exist there, not what the same servers cost.

options.text: Each Region keeps data inside unless you allow it out
options.why: Keeping data in place without permission is a security trait and does not explain a price gap.

labs.title: Survive an AZ outage
labs.brief: The owner wants the cafe's online ordering, order data included, kept in the Roastmere Region and running through an outage in any one of its three zones, for the fewest lab credits. Place each piece so at least two web servers stay behind the load balancer whichever zone fails, and the order data outlives any one zone. In this lab, two standard web servers carry the lunch rush (a lab value), each server and data piece runs in one zone, and the slot across all zones stays up when one fails.

containers.label: Across all Roastmere zones
containers.detail: Spans every zone of the Region

questions.stem: The cafe runs its ordering app in two Availability Zones of the Paris Region. A fire knocks out one zone, and the other zone keeps taking orders. Which facts about Availability Zones explain why the other zone kept running? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Each zone sits inside the area of a single Region.
options.why: Belonging to one Region is true of every zone but does nothing to shield one zone from a fire in another.

options.text: Each zone has its own power, networking and connectivity.
options.why: Independent power, networking and connectivity mean the fire's damage to one zone does not cut off the other.

options.text: Each zone holds one or more data centers of its own.
options.why: The data centers inside the burned zone go down with it, so holding data centers does not explain the survivor.

options.text: Each zone is kept physically apart from the other zones.
options.why: Zones are kept apart because one disaster can cut off a whole zone, so the fire stays in one place.

options.text: Each zone is placed close to the customers it serves.
options.why: Being near customers is about latency, which plays no part in surviving a fire in the other zone.

questions.takeaway: When one component fails and a standby steps in so downtime stays small, that is high availability.

questions.stem: The cafe runs its ordering app on a main server with a standby copy in a separate location. When the main server crashes during the lunch rush, the standby picks up the orders and customers barely notice a pause. Which property does this setup give the cafe?

options.text: High availability

options.text: Scalability
options.why: Scalability is about handling more load by adding capacity, not about surviving a crashed server.

options.text: Pay-as-you-go pricing
options.why: Paying only for what is used is a billing benefit and does nothing when the main server crashes.

options.text: Agility
options.why: Agility is about trying ideas and launching resources quickly, not about a standby taking over.

incidents.title: Launching the EU bean shop
incidents.brief: The cafe plans an online shop selling its roasted beans to shoppers across the EU. Before launch, the owner has to pick a Region for the shop, set a hosting budget and make sure the sign-up form follows the law.

steps.takeaway: A Region that lacks a service the workload needs fails the feature availability factor, however close it is.

read.text: The four factors are compliance, proximity, feature availability and pricing.

steps.stem: Most of the bean shop's buyers live near one EU Region, but a service the shop needs is still missing from that Region. Which Region selection factor rules that Region out?

options.text: Compliance with data protection law
options.why: Nothing in the scenario says a law bars that Region, so compliance is not what rules it out.

options.text: Proximity to most buyers
options.why: Being near most buyers counts in that Region's favor, so it cannot be what rules it out.

options.text: Feature availability
options.why: Services roll out to Regions gradually, and a Region that lacks a needed service cannot host the shop.

options.text: Pricing of local resources
options.why: The problem is a missing service, not what that Region charges for the ones it has.

steps.takeaway: AWS prices are published openly but differ by Region, so budget with the rates of the Region you will use.

read.text: AWS pricing is transparent and granular, yet each Region has its own rates.

steps.stem: The owner drafts the bean shop's hosting budget by reusing the server costs the cafe already pays in its US Region. Why might that budget be wrong for an EU Region?

options.text: AWS lists every charge openly
options.why: Openly listed charges let the owner look up the EU figures, but they do not explain why the US figures would differ.

options.text: Uptime is broadly equal across Regions
options.why: Equal uptime is about reliability, not cost, so it gives no reason for the budget to be off.

options.text: Each Region has its own rates
options.why: The same service can cost a different amount in each Region, so US prices may not match an EU Region.

options.text: Regions are walled off from each other
options.why: Isolation keeps data apart between Regions, but it says nothing about what each one charges.

steps.takeaway: Under GDPR, an EU online shop asks for consent before it collects anyone's personal data.

options.text: Data in a Region follows that country's law
options.why: This is true of every Region, but it is not a GDPR step the form takes before storing a sign-up.

options.text: The shopper must give consent up front
options.why: GDPR requires an EU online shop to get consent before it collects personal data, so the form must ask first.

options.text: Shoppers can later view or erase their own data
options.why: GDPR does give this right, but it applies once the details are stored, not before the form saves them.

options.text: Data leaves its Region only with your permission
options.why: Region isolation is an AWS security feature, not a GDPR rule the form must meet before storing details.

incidents.title: Rebuilding the cafe's setup in a new Region
incidents.brief: The cafe's ordering system took many days of console clicks to build in its home Region. Now the chain is opening in another country, and the team wants the same setup there without another round of manual work.

steps.takeaway: Mixing console clicks and ad hoc scripts lets Regions drift apart, which a single IaC blueprint avoids.

read.text: For consistent multi-Region rollouts, the console fits only small one-off jobs, scripts automate partly but get hard to maintain, and mixing methods causes drift.

steps.stem: Part of the team wants to rebuild the setup in the new Region by clicking through the console, while others want to patch together old scripts as they go. What problem does mixing these methods tend to cause?

options.text: Higher latency for distant customers
options.why: Latency comes from the distance between customers and a Region, and the build method does not change that distance.

options.text: Services not yet in the new Region
options.why: Features reach Regions gradually, so a missing service is a fact of the Region, not a result of mixing build methods.

options.text: Drift between the Regions' setups
options.why: Each method builds things a little differently, so the two Regions slowly stop matching.

options.text: Laws on where customer data lives
options.why: Data laws come with the new country and apply however the setup is built, so mixing methods does not cause them.

steps.takeaway: One CloudFormation template run in each Region builds identical environments with fewer errors.

read.text: One template across accounts or Regions gives identical environments from one command, with fewer errors and more resilience.

steps.stem: The team settles on AWS CloudFormation and plans to run the same template in the home Region and the new one. What does using that one template, rather than building by hand, give the team?

options.text: Rates set separately by each Region
options.why: Each Region charges its own rates whatever tool builds the resources, so the template does not bring this.

options.text: Content cached at edge locations
options.why: Caching content near customers is the job of edge locations, and CloudFormation is not a content cache.

options.text: Data that stays within its Region
options.why: Regions keep data apart unless the cafe allows it to cross, with or without a template, so this is not what the template adds.

options.text: Matching setups with fewer errors
options.why: Running one template in each Region builds matching environments without the slips of manual work.

steps.takeaway: A CloudFormation template is text declaring resources, so a change to it can be read and reviewed before it is built.

read.text: CloudFormation template: A text document declaring the resources to build.

steps.stem: Later, the cafe adds a cache cluster to its ordering system in both Regions. Before the change runs, the manager wants a teammate to read exactly what will change in the setup and sign off on it. Which property of the CloudFormation template makes that review practical?

options.text: It builds everything through AWS APIs
options.why: CloudFormation does build through AWS APIs, but that is how resources get made, not what lets a person read the change.

options.text: It is text that declares resources
options.why: A teammate can read the changed lines of a text declaration, so the new cache shows up plainly before anything is built.

options.text: It runs the same in every Region
options.why: Matching Regions is a benefit of one template, but it does not help a person see what this change adds.

options.text: It handles complex dependencies
options.why: CloudFormation can manage resources that depend on each other, but that does not make a change easier to read.

steps.takeaway: Scripted routine jobs run by developers, such as backups, use programmatic access through the AWS CLI or SDKs.

read.text: Programmatic access: Using AWS through code, with the AWS CLI or SDKs.

steps.stem: Separately, the cafe's developer wants a nightly job that backs up the new Region's Amazon EBS volumes from a script, with no browser involved. Which way of reaching AWS fits this job best?

options.text: Management Console access
options.why: The console is a browser tool for newcomers and simple workflows, not for a scripted nightly job.

options.text: Infrastructure as code
options.why: IaC declares the architecture for repeatable rollouts, while a routine backup job is a scripted task.

options.text: CloudShell access
options.why: AWS CloudShell is a terminal opened in the browser, so it needs the browser this job is meant to avoid.

options.text: Programmatic access
options.why: Using AWS through code, such as AWS CLI commands in a script, suits a routine scheduled backup.
